units.translation: Hesychius: άελπτοι [unhoped-for, unexpected]: δεινοί [terrible], and ἄαπτοι [untouchable]. Aeschylus in Proteus (fr. 211). Aeschylus seems to have said either ἄεπτοι [unhoped-for] or, more probably, ἄαπτοι [untouchable], which is known from the Homeric (Il. 1, 567) χεῖρας ἀάπτους [untouchable hands] as a variant reading, which perhaps similarly existed in Aeschylus' Proteus, but the truth is undoubtedly ἄαπτοι [untouchable], as in the Homeric passage Aristarchus approved ἀάπτους [untouchable] (with the rough breathing, which means χεῖρας ὧν οὐκ ἂν ἅψαιτό τις [hands that no one would touch]). || The copyist's error who wrote ἄεπτα [unhoped-for] for ελπτα in Suppl. 911 I noted under the word ἄελπτος [unhoped-for]. || In another way there is an error in the verses Ag. 140-141 written thus in M: τόσσων περ εὔφρων καλά | δρόσοισιν ἀέλπτοις μαλερῶν ὄντων [of so many, kindly, beautiful things, with unhoped-for dews of fierce ones], which I have shown in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. LXXXIV-LXXXVI should be emended thus: ὄσσων παρ᾽ εὐφρόνων καλὰ Διὸς κόρα | δρόσοισιν μαλερῶν τε λεόντων [from kindly eyes, beautiful daughter of Zeus, with dews of fierce lions]. The scholiast either read or wanted to read ἀέπτοις [unhoped-for] for αέλπτοις. For on δρόσοισιν [dews] in M is annotated: τοῖς νεογνοῖς [to the newborn] "χωρίς δ᾽ αὖτ᾽ ἔρσαι" [and apart from them the dew] (Hom. Od. 9, 222) ἀέλπτοις [unhoped-for] (so the codex, against the scholiast's intention) but τοῖς ἕπεσθαι τοῖς γονεῦσι μὴ δυναμένοις [to those unable to follow their parents]. The first part of this annotation was written by an old grammarian, as is understood from Etym. M. p. 377, 37, where the noun δρόσων [dews] is similarly compared with the Homeric ἔρσαι [dews], for ἔρση γάρ ἐστιν ἡ δρόσος [for dew is the dew]. And Aeschylus in Agamemnon called the cubs of lions δρόσους [dews], translating this. But the other part of the scholium, in which ἀέπτοις [unhoped-for] is explained, is the invention of a more recent grammarian, who had not noticed that this word had been rashly introduced into this verse, which opinion is also confirmed by the fact that in the codex δρόσοισιν [dews] is written, not δρόσοις [dews], which Triclinius put, so that the beginning of the verse would be iambic. Nor is the tenderness of lion cubs so great as that of birds scarcely hatched from the egg, that it could have seemed worthwhile to Aeschylus to add to the noun δρόσων [dews], which itself already contains the notion of tenderness, some epithet of that sort. Truly ridiculous is the Byzantine scholiast, who interpreted ἀέπτοις [unhoped-for] as τοῖς μὴ δυναμένοις πτῆναι [to those unable to fly], as if lions, which today are accustomed to walk on four feet, flew in the age of Aeschylus: unless perhaps the clever fellow wanted it to be said figuratively, just as Sophocles OR. 17 called infants οὐδέπω πτέσθαι σθένοντας [not yet able to fly], with a comparison drawn from νεοσσοῖς [chicks], by which name infants are often called by poets. It is manifest that this ἀέπτοις [unhoped-for] was corrupted from an old gloss ἀετοῖς [eagles], which was once written next to the words in v. 136 πτανοῖσιν κυσί πατρός [winged dogs of the father]: about which I have said more in Fleckeisen's Annals, year 1863, vol. 87, p. 75-79.
unhoped-for: terrible, and untouchable. Aeschylus in Proteus
